## James 3 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Context Overview

James 3 is the third in a series of "tests of living faith" (Guzik, MacArthur). Chapter 2 tested faith by works; chapter 3 tests faith by words. "In James 2 the question is do your works match your words ('I believe'), and in James 3 the question is do your words match your words ('I am a believer')." — Precept Austin

The chapter falls into two sections: vv. 1–12 on the tongue, and vv. 13–18 on true versus false wisdom.

---

### v. 1 — "Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly."

**Traditional Reading**

James is not forbidding the teaching office but warning against rushing into it lightly. The early church allowed many to teach in turn, and the office carried prestige (Gill notes the Jewish love of being called "Rabbi, Rabbi"). James says "Stop becoming many teachers" (present imperative with negative), implying too many were taking up the role without considering the cost.

— Guzik / Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-3/

The reason is a "stricter judgment" (Greek *meizon krima* — a greater sentence). James includes himself in the "we," a mark of humility. Gill explains teachers will be judged "out of their own mouths" — if they teach one thing and live another, their own words condemn them. The Pulpit Commentary cross-references Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47 where Jesus says some "shall receive greater condemnation."

— Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/3.htm
— Pulpit (searched excerpt): https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/3.htm

MacArthur says: "To sin with the tongue when alone or with one or two other persons is bad enough; but to sin with the tongue in public, especially while acting as a speaker for God, is immeasurably worse." — Precept Austin quoting MacArthur: https://www.preceptaustin.org/james-3-commentary

**Baptist Perspective** (MacArthur / GTY): Speech is the mark of true faith; therefore teachers, who depend on speech, are held to a higher standard. "A faith which does not transform the tongue is no saving faith at all." — Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/james-3-commentary

**Reformed Perspective** (Ferguson / Desiring God): "Teachers should be conscious of the weight and potential influence of what they say because words lie at the heart of the teaching ministry. The potential for multiplication of influence requires a canon of judgment that takes the measure of both responsibility and opportunity into account." — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-tongue-the-bridle-and-the-blessing-an-exposition-of-james-3-1-12

---

### v. 2 — "We all stumble in many ways. If anyone is never at fault in what he says, he is a perfect man, able to control his whole body."

**Traditional Reading**

"For" (*gar*) links this to v. 1: teachers face stricter judgment *because* all stumble, and teachers stumble most easily with words. "Stumble" (*ptaiō*) does not mean a fatal fall but a trip that hinders progress (Guzik). James includes himself — "we all stumble" — no exceptions (Bengel: "No se ipsos quidem excipiunt apostoli" — not even the apostles except themselves).

— Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-3/
— Pulpit (searched): https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/3.htm

The "perfect" (*teleios*) man is not sinlessly perfect. Gill says either (a) hypothetically — if such a person existed he would be perfect — or (b) the word means mature, complete, fully developed. MacArthur agrees: "perfect" describes those who are spiritually mature and thus able to control their tongues. — Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/james-3-commentary

The tongue is the indicator of the heart. As Ferguson puts it, "What comes out of our mouths is usually an accurate index of the health of our hearts" — like a doctor asking you to stick out your tongue. — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-tongue-the-bridle-and-the-blessing-an-exposition-of-james-3-1-12

**Baptist** (Spurgeon, quoted in Enduring Word and Precept Austin): "If religion does not salt your tongue, and keep it sweet, it has done nothing for you. If the doctor wants to know the state of your health, he says, 'Let me see your tongue'; and there is no better test of the health of the mind than to see what is on the tongue." — Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/james-3-commentary

---

### v. 3 — "When we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we can guide the whole animal."

**Traditional Reading**

The first of two illustrations of disproportionate influence. The bit is tiny compared to the horse, yet it controls the whole animal. Gill notes horses "are without understanding, and need direction" — the bit-and-bridle gives the rider control. Similarly, a bridled tongue directs the whole body.

— Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/3.htm
— Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-3/

Guzik adds an important question: "Who or what holds the reins?" The Spirit of God must direct the tongue; otherwise emotions or the carnal nature steer it. — Guzik

Ferguson: "The tongue is like the bit in the mouth of a horse. This tiny appliance controls the enormous power and energy of the horse and is used to give it direction." — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-tongue-the-bridle-and-the-blessing-an-exposition-of-james-3-1-12

---

### v. 4 — "Consider ships as well. Although they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot is inclined."

**Traditional Reading**

The second illustration. Ancient ships could be enormous — Ferguson notes the *Isis* could carry 1,000 people, and Paul's ship held 276 (Acts 27:37). Yet a tiny rudder turns it. Gill cites Aristotle's *Mechanica*, which marvels at "a small helm" steering a great ship. James' point: the tongue, like the rudder, is tiny but decisive in its effect.

— Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/3.htm
— Ferguson: https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-tongue-the-bridle-and-the-blessing-an-exposition-of-james-3-1-12

Guzik: "You don't solve the problem of an unruly horse by keeping it in the barn, or the problem of a hard-to-steer ship by keeping it tied to the dock. In the same way, even a vow of silence is not the ultimate answer." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-3/

---

### v. 5 — "In the same way, the tongue is a small part of the body, but it boasts of great things. Consider how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze."

**Traditional Reading**

The tongue "boasts of great things" — Gill notes this can be taken in a good sense (a sanctified tongue speaks great things like the Gospel) but the context of vv. 5b–6 shifts to the destructive potential. The wildfire illustration: a tiny spark can destroy a vast forest. Burdick (quoted by Guzik): the bit and rudder control, but the spark destroys — the tongue can do either.

— Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/3.htm
— Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-3/

---

### v. 6 — "The tongue also is a fire, a world of wickedness among the parts of the body. It pollutes the whole person, sets the course of his life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell."

**Traditional Reading**

This is the most theologically dense verse in the passage. James piles up images:

- **"A fire"**: destructive, spreading, consuming. Gill: like fire it devours all in its path — "devouring words" (Ps 52:4). Proverbs 26:20–21: as wood feeds fire, whisperers and talebearers feed strife.
- **"A world of wickedness"**: Gill: "as the world is full of things, and full of sin… so is the tongue full of iniquity." The rabbis said an evil tongue equals idolatry, adultery, and murder combined. — Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/3.htm
- **"Pollutes the whole person"**: the tongue stains the entire body like a spot on a wedding dress (Ferguson). — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-tongue-the-bridle-and-the-blessing-an-exposition-of-james-3-1-12
- **"Sets on fire the course of nature"** — literally "the wheel of birth" (*ton trochon tēs geneseōs*). Gill: this may refer to the whole course of a person's life from birth, or the cycle of generations. The tongue can set a whole life ablaze.
- **"Set on fire by hell"** — Greek *Gehenna*, the Valley of Hinnom, Jerusalem's perpetually burning rubbish dump. Ferguson: "It is from such a hell that destructive words arise. Remember that imagery whenever similar words seek to force their way out of your mouth." — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-tongue-the-bridle-and-the-blessing-an-exposition-of-james-3-1-12

Gill cites the Talmud: "Whoever uses an evil tongue, the holy blessed God says to hell, I concerning him above, and thou concerning him below, will judge him." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/3.htm

**Note**: The phrase "course of nature" / "wheel of birth" is difficult. The Pulpit Commentary sees it as the round of human life. Some modern scholars suggest it means "the whole of one's life from birth." I was unable to fetch the netbible.org notes to check their position.

---

### vv. 7–8 — "All kinds of animals, birds, reptiles, and creatures of the sea are being tamed and have been tamed by man, but no man can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison."

**Traditional Reading**

James echoes the Genesis creation categories (beasts, birds, reptiles, sea creatures). Mankind has subdued them all (Genesis 1:28). Yet "no man can tame the tongue." Gill: this means no one can tame his own or others' tongues by human power alone; only God by His Spirit and grace can do it.

— Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/3.htm

"Restless evil" (*akatastaton kakon*) — the same word as "unstable" in James 1:8 (the double-minded man). Ferguson connects this: the restless tongue mimics Satan, who "goes to and fro throughout the earth" (Job 1:7), "like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour" (1 Peter 5:8). — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-tongue-the-bridle-and-the-blessing-an-exposition-of-james-3-1-12

"Full of deadly poison" — Ferguson hears an echo of Genesis 3 and the serpent's deadly deceit. Paul quotes Psalm 5:9: "the venom of asps is under their lips" (Romans 3:13). — Ferguson

Guzik adds: only God is mightier than the human tongue. "No man can tame the tongue. Nevertheless the tongue can be brought under the power and the control of the Holy Spirit." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-3/

**Pentecostal / Charismatic** (Enduring Word / David Guzik): The emphasis falls on the Holy Spirit as the only power able to tame the tongue. This aligns with Pentecostal emphasis on Spirit-empowered sanctification.

---

### v. 9 — "With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in God's likeness."

**Traditional Reading**

The same instrument used for the highest act (blessing God) is used for the lowest (cursing people made in His image). Gill calls this "monstrous and shocking." The point is sharpened by "made in God's likeness" — to curse a person is to attack the image of God.

— Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/3.htm
— Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-3/

Guzik notes Peter epitomized this contradiction: he confessed Jesus as Messiah with the same tongue he used to deny Jesus with curses. — Guzik

---

### vv. 10–12 — "Out of the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, this should not be! Can both fresh water and salt water flow from the same spring? My brothers, can a fig tree grow olives, or a grapevine bear figs? Neither can a salt spring produce fresh water."

**Traditional Reading**

James issues a sharp rebuke: "this should not be!" (*ou chrē tauta houtōs ginesthai* — "these things ought not so to be"). Gill says such contradiction is unbecoming of the Christian name. — Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/3.htm

The three nature illustrations (spring, fig tree, grapevine) all make the same point: a thing produces according to its nature. Ferguson: "Forked tongue connected to forked heart. Such speech is a mark of the 'double-minded man' who is 'unstable in all his ways' (James 1:8)." — https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-tongue-the-bridle-and-the-blessing-an-exposition-of-james-3-1-12

Guzik, quoting Spurgeon: "It would be a monstrosity… if a fig tree started bearing olive berries, and it is just as unnatural for a Christian to live in sin." Spurgeon adds pointedly: "Unless you are regenerated, born from above by a new and heavenly birth, you are not Christians, whatever you may be called." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-3/

**Reformed / Spurgeon**: The fig-and-olive illustration presses the perseverance / regeneration point: if bitter water keeps flowing, the spring is bad. True regeneration changes the nature of the source.

---

### v. 13 — "Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show it by his good conduct, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom."

**Traditional Reading**

The transition from tongue to wisdom is natural: "all this evil springs from a vain opinion men have of their own wisdom" (Gill). James now contrasts two wisdoms.

*Sophos* ("wise") was the technical term for a rabbi or teacher among the Jews (Burdick, cited by Guzik). James is still addressing would-be teachers: it's not just what they say but how they live. — Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-3/

True wisdom is demonstrated, not merely claimed. "Wisdom is not mere head knowledge. Real wisdom and understanding will show in our lives, by our good conduct." — Guzik

"Meekness of wisdom" (*prautēti sophias*): meekness is not weakness. Burdick (quoted by Guzik): "It is an active attitude of deliberate acceptance." — Guzik

The Pulpit Commentary notes that *epistēmōn* ("understanding") is found only here in the NT and in the LXX is paired with *sophos* (Deut 1:13; 4:6). It means one who understands and knows, while *sophos* is one who carries knowledge into life. — Pulpit (searched): https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/3.htm

---

### vv. 14–16 — "But if you harbor bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast in it or deny the truth. Such wisdom does not come from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every evil practice."

**Traditional Reading**

"Bitter jealousy" (*zēlon pikron*) and "selfish ambition" (*eritheian*) — the latter originally meant "working for hire," then factionalism, party-spirit. Moffatt (quoted by Guzik): "It is out of keeping with the temper of bitter jealousy and rivalry (i.e., party-spirit, selfish ambition, factiousness)." — Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-3/

Three adjectives describe false wisdom:

1. **Earthly** (*epigeios*): "Having this life only in view" (Clarke, via Guzik). Evaluates everything by worldly standards.
2. **Unspiritual / sensual** (*psychikē*): The Pulpit Commentary gives an extended note on this rare word (6x in NT). It means "animal" or "natural" — ruled by the *psychē* (lower soul) rather than the Spirit. It is "the wisdom of the flesh." The Pulpit notes that *psychikos* is "in every instance a most depreciatory" term. — Pulpit (searched): https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/3.htm
3. **Demonic** (*daimoniōdēs*): "Inspired by demons, and maintained in the soul by their indwelling influence" (Clarke, via Guzik). — Guzik

The outcome: "disorder" (*akatastasia*) and "every evil practice." The Pulpit notes this is the opposite of the peace and order that characterise God's work. — Pulpit (searched)

**Reformed** (Ligonier / Desiring God articles — searched but not fully fetched): The Desiring God article on "Can You Still Be Persuaded?" notes that the absence of heavenly wisdom is not mere ignorance but to be "earthly, unspiritual, [and] demonic." Wisdom here is moral, not merely intellectual. — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/can-you-still-be-persuaded

---

### v. 17 — "But the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peace-loving, gentle, accommodating, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial, and sincere."

**Traditional Reading**

This is one of the great character-description passages of the NT, comparable to Paul's fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:22–23) and love chapter (1 Cor 13). Ellicott says: "Whereas, in sweetest contrast to all this repulsive foulness and riot, the true wisdom from above is first pure, chaste as the Lamb of God." — Ellicott (searched): https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/james/3.htm

The seven (or eight) qualities:

1. **First pure** (*hagnē*): not primarily sexual but "the absence of any sinful attitude or motive" (Burdick, via Guzik). Purity comes first; peace without purity is false peace. Plumptre: "purity must be secured even at the expense of peace." — Pulpit (searched)
2. **Peace-loving** (*eirēnikē*): in the LXX this word is used mostly of God's disposition as King — "gentle and kind, although in reality He has every reason to be stern and punitive" (Burdick, via Guzik).
3. **Gentle** (*epieikēs*): Barclay calls this "sweet reasonableness" — "the man who knows when it is actually wrong to apply the strict letter of the law." — Guzik
4. **Accommodating / willing to yield** (*eupeithēs*): "not stubborn nor obstinate; of a yielding disposition in all indifferent things" (Clarke, via Guzik). Not weak pliability but willingness to listen to reason.
5. **Full of mercy and good fruit**: does not judge strictly by law; extends mercy knowing "the same measure of mercy we grant to others is the same measure God will use with us" (Matt 7:2). — Guzik
6. **Impartial** (*adiakritos*): "without judging, i.e., either a curious inquiring into the faults of others, to find matter for censures" (Poole, via Guzik). Or "without partiality."
7. **Sincere** (*anypokritos*): "without hypocrisy" — "without pretending to be what it is not; acting always in its own character" (Clarke, via Guzik).

— Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-3/

Ferguson references the "open to reason" translation of *eupeithēs*, connecting it to being persuadable — a mark of genuine Christian humility (Proverbs 18:17). — Desiring God article: https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/can-you-still-be-persuaded

**Methodist / Wesleyan** (Seedbed.com — not fetched due to limits): I was unable to access Wesleyan teaching on this passage. Wesley's own notes on James 3 are available at wesley.nnu.edu but could not be retrieved in this session.

**Lutheran** (LCMS.org / 1517.org — not fetched due to limits): I was unable to access Lutheran commentary on this text.

### v. 18 — "Peacemakers who sow in peace reap the fruit of righteousness."

**Traditional Reading**

This verse echoes the Beatitude: "Blessed are the peacemakers" (Matt 5:9). The Pulpit Commentary calls it "St. James's version of the beatitude." — Pulpit (searched): https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/james/3.htm

"The fruit of righteousness" is an OT phrase (Prov 11:30; Amos 6:12; also Phil 1:11). Gill says righteousness is "sown in peace by the peacemaker, and produces it." — Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/james/3.htm

The phrase *tois poiousin eirēnēn* can mean either "for them that make peace" or "by them that make peace" (Pulpit). Either way, peaceable sowing yields a harvest of righteousness.

Guzik: "This fruit is like a seed that will bear fruit as it is sown by those who make peace." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/james-3/

## Denominational Distinctives (Where Found)

Given tooling limits, I was unable to retrieve full content from several sources. However, from what was obtained:

- **Baptist** (MacArthur / GTY / Spurgeon): Heavily emphasises the tongue as a *test of saving faith*. If faith doesn't transform speech, it's not saving faith. Spurgeon ties the fig/olive illustration directly to regeneration: a changed nature is required, not just external labelling.

- **Reformed** (Ferguson / Desiring God): Emphasises the tongue as evidence of *spiritual maturity* and the forked tongue as the mark of the "double-minded man" (James 1:8). The law's work is to stop every mouth (Rom 3:19) before grace opens it for blessing. Focus on sanctification as a long, daily battle.

- **Pentecostal / Charismatic** (Guzik / Enduring Word): Strong emphasis on the Holy Spirit as the *only* power that can tame the tongue ("only God Himself is mightier than the human tongue"). The solution is not human effort but Spirit-empowered control.

---

## Other Views

**Catholic and Orthodox**: I was unable to retrieve content from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org due to search/fetch limits. The Catholic epistles are part of the canon for all traditions, and James is especially significant in Catholic theology for its emphasis on works. The Vulgate's rendering of v. 1 (*sumitis* — "you receive" greater judgment, missing James's self-inclusive "we") was noted by the Pulpit Commentary as a mistranslation.

**Modern Scholarship**: I was unable to fetch netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org notes due to tooling limits.
